clue.text: A hundred meet a Delphic celebrity in the craft

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
the oracle at Delphi was the most famous in ancient Greece

explanation.surface: A centenarian visits a famous Delphic seer aboard some boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the' only links the wordplay to the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A coracle is a small round wicker boat, a kind of small vessel or craft.

clue.text: Where to place us, as the spacemen might say

definitions.text: Where to place us, as the spacemen might say

indicators.note: the letters of place us are rearranged into the word that astronauts would use for their craft

explanation.surface: Astronauts describe the spot where they are to be put.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of PLACE US rearrange into the answer, signalled by 'as the spacemen might say', and the whole clue describes the spacecraft astronauts ride in.
explanation.definitionFit: The sealed cabin of a spacecraft is where astronauts are placed.

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gunners
taken as written
a proof is a demonstration that something is true

explanation.surface: Artillerymen take part in a display of toughness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' supplies its own letters rather than putting one piece inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Something impermeable lets no water through, so it keeps out showers.

parts.note: the City street called ..., a name made of a word plus 'side'

explanation.surface: A district on one edge of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheapside is a street in the City of London; the answer is the part before 'side'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapside means the market side, and its first part is the word for inexpensive.

parts.note: a fill-in from Hamlet's reply to Polonius when asked whether he knows him

explanation.surface: A line from Hamlet in which the prince insults Polonius.
explanation.walkthrough: The feed ran clue 3 into this one; the page prints only the quotation. Hamlet's line is 'Excellent well; you are a fishmonger'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's adverb modifying 'well' means extremely, used as an intensifier in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Encumbered when going south ? Too bad !

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
an addled egg is one gone too bad to eat, rotten

explanation.surface: Someone loaded down as they head south, and it is a pity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too bad!' reads as an exclamation of sympathy, but it describes a rotten egg.
explanation.definitionFit: To be saddled with something is to be burdened or weighed down by it.

parts.note: a US term for drawing fabric into parallel rows of gathers

explanation.surface: A convention of the American cloth trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gathering' suggests a meeting, but it is the needlework sense, gathers in cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: In America this word names decorative gathering of fabric on threads.

clue.text: Dreary Mod: enough to give one the hump !

definitions.text: Dreary Mod: enough to give one the hump !

indicators.text: enough to give one the hump
indicators.note: to have the hump is to be upset, so the words Dreary Mod are upset into a new order

explanation.surface: A dull youth in sixties fashion is irritating enough to annoy anybody.
explanation.walkthrough: DREARY MOD rearranges into the answer, signalled by 'enough to give one the hump', and the one-humped camel is the whole clue's picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabian camel carries a single hump on its back.
The word means reclining flat and also uttering falsehoods.

parts.note: swimmers dive in at the pool's deepest part, and to go off at that part is to lose one's temper

explanation.surface: A place for enthusiastic divers.
explanation.walkthrough: Going off the deep end means losing one's temper, hence 'impassioned'.
explanation.definitionFit: Divers jump in where the pool is deepest, and the idiom of going off there means flying into a passion.

parts.note: a group of lions has a collective noun, and Jane Austen's novel title loses its second half, 'and Prejudice'

explanation.surface: Famous writers who judge nobody fairly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary lions' suggests celebrated authors, but the lions are real animals in a group, and the literature is Austen's title with 'and Prejudice' removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A family group of lions is called a pride, and Austen's novel is Pride and Prejudice.

parts.note: fashion for someone wearing hoops: a Victorian skirt held out by a frame of hoops

explanation.surface: The dress designs of somebody called Hooper.
explanation.walkthrough: Hooper looks like a surname, but it means a wearer of hoops.
explanation.definitionFit: A crinoline is a stiff petticoat or hooped frame worn under a Victorian skirt, a garment of fashion.

parts.note: Hamlet's phrase for something too refined for the common people, who do not enjoy it

explanation.surface: Something resembling fish roe served to an army officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The general' is not an army officer but, in Hamlet's sense, the general public.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wasted on ordinary people because they do not like it lacks popular appeal.

parts.note: Solomon ... was the mad Quaker who preached naked through plague-stricken London, and his surname is a bird of prey

explanation.surface: Someone tells a man called Solomon he is a madcap.
explanation.walkthrough: Solomon Eagle (or Eccles), a seventeenth-century fanatic, appears as a madman in Defoe's Journal of the Plague Year; 'bird' gives the surname a second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The raptor of the same name gave the crazed preacher his surname, so one word covers both bird and madman.

clue.text: Use attrition tactics in the rodeo

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words 'the rodeo', running across them

explanation.surface: A cowboy wears down an opponent during a rodeo contest.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear something away gradually is to grind it down by attrition.

clue.text: Bolting that bolting might have prevented?

definitions.text: Bolting that bolting might have prevented?

parts.words: Bolting that bolting might have prevented
parts.note: running off to marry in secret, which a locked door might have stopped

explanation.surface: An escape that locking the door would have stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'bolting' is fleeing; the second is fastening a door.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple running away to marry secretly is a kind of bolting.

parts.note: auricular means of the ear, so this is identified by a mark on the ear, as farm animals are

explanation.surface: Someone famous for their ears.
explanation.walkthrough: Livestock are identified by a nick or tag in the ear; the word now means set aside for a purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals marked on the ear for identity gave the word for reserving something for a particular use.

clue.text: Place for left-wing reprimand reserved for V.I.P.s

parts.note: red is the colour of the political left
to carpet someone is to call them in for a reprimand

explanation.surface: Somewhere a socialist is told off, kept for important visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' as a verb means to scold, from being called onto the boss's carpet; 'reserved for V.I.P.s' describes the definition's place.
explanation.definitionFit: The ceremonial rug laid out for distinguished guests is a place kept for celebrities.

definitions.meaning: seized and carried someone off by force
the novel by Stevenson that came before his sequel Catriona

explanation.definitionFit: The word means abducted and is the title of Stevenson's novel to which Catriona is the sequel.

indicators.note: the words after fond are given treatment, worked over into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone feels slighted after being handled too affectionately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treatment' signals that AFTER FOND is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To be affronted is to be offended by an open slight.

parts.note: learning to become a skilled manual worker; the letters of train as also rearrange to give the word

explanation.surface: Someone learns a manual trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of TRAIN AS rearrange into the answer, though no word signals the rearrangement, as older puzzles allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanic in the old sense is a skilled manual worker or craftsman.

clue.text: Make music at the highest level

definitions.text: Make music at the highest level

parts.words: Make music at the highest level
parts.note: singing up in the mountains, in the warbling style of Alpine herdsmen

explanation.surface: A top-flight musician performs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Highest level' sounds like excellence but means high altitude: the Alpine song.
explanation.definitionFit: Swiss and Tyrolean mountain dwellers sing in rapid switches between chest voice and falsetto.

clue.text: Homer returning in a haughty manner ?

definitions.text: Homer returning in a haughty manner ?

parts.words: Homer returning in a haughty manner
parts.note: a homer is a homing pigeon, which flies back to its loft

explanation.surface: The Greek poet comes back with a proud air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homer' looks like the Greek poet but is a homing pigeon returning to its loft.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means haughtily, and it sounds like a pigeon's way back to the loft.

clue.text: Out East its topping work in the sandhill

definitions.text: Out East its topping work in the sandhill

parts.words: Out East its topping work in the sandhill
parts.note: in India it is headgear, something worn on top, and a golfer topping a ball from a tee, once a little hill of sand, suggests the same sound

explanation.surface: In the Orient someone does excellent work among the dunes.
explanation.walkthrough: Topping a ball is hitting its top, a poor golf shot; early golf tees were pinches of sand, so 'topping work in the sandhill' is a top tee.
explanation.definitionFit: A pith helmet worn against the sun in India is a light hat, so out East it covers the top.

parts.note: a single spike of a fork or pitchfork, and also one line of a several-sided assault

explanation.surface: A single target in a military offensive.
explanation.definitionFit: A tine of a fork is one point, and a multi-pronged attack has several lines.

parts.note: not a soldier carrying colours but the pole that holds up a flag

explanation.surface: A person who carries a regiment's flag.
explanation.walkthrough: A standard-bearer is usually a person; here it is the pole itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall pole from which a banner flies literally bears the standard.

clue.text: Raid causes a fight about nothing

indicators.note: the word for a fight is put about, around, the nothing

parts.note: a fray is a fight or brawl
O is the round figure for nothing

explanation.surface: An attack leads to a brawl over a trifle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts FRAY around O.
explanation.definitionFit: A foray is a sudden attack or sortie into enemy ground.

clue.text: It can be close to the plinth

indicators.note: close can be made into another word by rearranging its letters

explanation.surface: Something might be standing near the base of a statue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' signals that CLOSE is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A socle is a low block or base supporting a column or statue.

parts.note: a rock specialist would harvest a yield of rocks, and that is also the name of a sedum plant

explanation.surface: A specimen of greenery belonging to an earth scientist.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant is a low succulent (sedum) that grows on rocks and walls.
explanation.definitionFit: The succulent sedum growing on walls and rocks has a name meaning a harvest of rocks.

parts.note: the emperor Tiberius spent his last years in retreat on an island in the Bay of Naples

explanation.surface: A holiday spot connected with a Roman emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bay of Naples island where Tiberius built villas is still a holiday destination.

clue.text: " And - - to the listening Earth Repeats the story of her birth" (Addison)

definitions.text: " And - - to the listening Earth Repeats the story of her birth" (Addison)

parts.words: " And - - to the listening Earth Repeats the story of her birth" (Addison)
parts.note: a fill-in from Addison's hymn The Spacious Firmament, in which the moon tells her tale to the earth each evening

explanation.surface: A line of verse about the moon telling the earth her history.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word comes from Addison's hymn 'The spacious firmament on high'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means every evening, how often the moon tells her story.

parts.note: the nursery rhyme about Solomon Grundy, born on Monday, gives the next day for his christening

explanation.surface: The date a man named Solomon was baptised.
explanation.walkthrough: Solomon is not the biblical king but Solomon Grundy of the nursery rhyme: 'Born on a Monday, christened on Tuesday'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme gives the second weekday as the day of the christening.
